title: Motion Preferences and Accessibility
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of motion preferences and accessibility.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on motion preferences and accessibility and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Motion Preferences and Accessibility matters because interface appearance should reflect actual state while remaining understandable to keyboard, touch and assistive-technology users.

content_blocks.title: Module 13 learning map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step module learning map: Transform Utilities → Transition Duration and Timing → Scroll and Snap Utilities → Advanced Visual Effects. Lesson pages add code examples and practice.
content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 13, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Reduced-motion media preferences; Reducing unnecessary movement; Keeping interactions understandable without animation; Preserving essential state feedback. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Motion Preferences and Accessibility
content_blocks.code:
<button class="rounded-lg bg-blue-700 px-4 py-2 text-white focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-700 motion-reduce:transition-none">
  Save changes
</button>
content_blocks.expected_output: The control has a visible keyboard focus indicator and suppresses nonessential transitions for reduced-motion users.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to motion preferences and accessibility, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating motion preferences and accessibility. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to motion preferences and accessibility.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to motion preferences and accessibility.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: The control has a visible keyboard focus indicator and suppresses nonessential transitions for reduced-motion users.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying motion preferences and accessibility without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Motion Preferences and Accessibility is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
